html:
We define control primitives as the reusable algorithmic operations that coordinate behavior under uncertainty, goals, and context. These include basic subroutines for selectively loading information into working memory, maintaining or clearing it, monitoring and adjusting competing demands, and routing information through neural circuits. For example, fronto-striatal "gating" circuits implement working-memory update and maintenance: cortical inputs are allowed into active prefrontal representations only when striatal "Go" signals disinhibit corresponding regions of the thalamus. Computational models show that nested prefrontal-basal ganglia loops can implement distinct input and output gates, as well as a "reset" to clear outdated contents 1. Recent neural-network models confirm that dorsolateral PFC populations can re-use the same neurons to store multiple items by strategic gating, trading off slot-like capacity for precision under dopamine-modulated learning 2. In these models, striatal D1/D2 circuitry (go/no-go pathways) controls fronto-thalamic gating, while phasic dopamine (reward-prediction errors) adaptively tunes which items are gated or maintained. This cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop effectively acts as a control primitive for selective updating of working memory, and will be covered in greater depth in Section X. A 2025 computational model extends the PBWM framework (Figure).

Other primitives govern switching and stopping of actions or rules. Task-set switching engages frontoparietal and basal ganglia loops to reconfigure task rules and contexts, analogous to motor set switches. By contrast, action stopping taps a well-characterized hyperdirect pathway: when an unexpected stop signal appears, right inferior frontal cortex (rIFC, sometimes called rIFG) and pre-SMA rapidly drive the subthalamic nucleus (STN), which in turn excites globus pallidus output to globally inhibit thalamocortical circuits. This PFC-STN "brake" can halt ongoing motor plans. Human ECoG and stimulation studies show that potentials in rIFC precede STN activation during stopping, and individuals with stronger rIFC-STN coupling stop faster 3. In rodents, optogenetic excitation of STN (or of the dmPFC->STN pathway) causally delays or interrupts responses, confirming its key role. Notably, stopping is associated with transient frontal beta-band bursts (in rIFC/preSMA and STN), suggesting that brief oscillatory events implement the top-down "stop" command. Thus, the stop primitive is instantiated by a PFC-basal ganglia loop that can globally suspend output. The 2025 model simulates a sequence of gating decisions (Figure).

Conflict monitoring and uncertainty are also treated as control primitives: medial frontal cortex, especially dorsal ACC, signals when processing conflicts or errors rise, triggering adjustments in control. Theoretical models propose that ACC computes the "expected value of control" by integrating anticipated rewards, required effort, and uncertainty, then biasing when and how much to engage executive mechanisms 4. Empirically, ACC activity correlates with conflict levels, error likelihood and volatility, and predicts the need to upregulate lateral PFC control. Thus, a conflict-monitoring primitive may reside in ACC, detecting when parallel responses or surprising outcomes demand increased top-down control.

Another primitive is decision-threshold modulation: adjusting response speed-accuracy tradeoffs. Here the basal ganglia again play a role. For example, activity in the STN can raise decision thresholds during conflict (through diffusely inhibiting motor output) 5, 6, whereas striatal Go/No-Go balance can shift the threshold of gating 7. Dopamine likewise influences threshold: high tonic dopamine can bias faster decisions (lower effective threshold), whereas dips can induce caution 8. These mechanisms allow flexible control of when to commit versus continue deliberating.

A related primitive is meta-control, the arbitration between decision systems (e.g. model-based vs. model-free, or goal-directed vs. habitual) based on uncertainty or task demands. Here cortical-striatal loops again are key. Ventromedial circuits (OFC, ventral striatum) tend to encode predicted reward outcomes (model-based planning) 9, whereas dorsolateral striatal loops execute learned habits 10, 11, 12. Some evidence (e.g. from neural decoding in primates) suggests higher PFC areas monitor reliability of each system and gate which one drives action 13, 14, 15. In effect, meta-control might be implemented by gating which striatal loop is currently dominant, influenced by dopamine (and perhaps serotonin) context signals 16, 17, 18, 19, though the precise "arbitrator" circuitry is still under study 20.

Finally, a fundamental primitive is information routing and shielding. Prefrontal networks must selectively broadcast current goals or rules to task-relevant modules while protecting them from interference. Recent work highlights the role of the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus 21, 22: MD nuclei form recurrent loops with PFC and can transiently amplify or redirect PFC representations. In rodents, disrupting MD input to PFC impairs flexible working memory and set-shifting 23, 24. Theoretical and empirical studies suggest MD acts like a dynamic switchboard, enabling a given PFC population to drive its targets when needed. In short, thalamocortical loops provide primitives for gating communication between cortical areas and for holding information "in the blackboard" against distractors 25.
